title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems were deployed to create fake interviews and deepfake content impersonating real public figures and financial experts, intended to direct victims toward unlicensed investment platforms. The deployment was entirely outside any legitimate use case, as the system was used by fraudsters to generate content designed to deceive rather than inform. This failure could only have been caught by the platforms hosting the content, through verification that interviews actually occurred and cross-reference with the impersonated figures' actual statements and appearances.

The specific failure mode is impersonation at scale. A fake interview between Alan Kohler and Michele Bullock was published as if real, and deepfake images and videos of celebrities, politicians, and financial figures were used to promote unlicensed trading platforms. ASIC reports that such AI-generated scams rose sharply, with 19,400 scams removed in one year, including thousands of fake investment platforms and phishing operations. The most commonly impersonated figures included Kohler, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, and billionaire Gina Rinehart.

It is not established whether the AI systems used were purpose-built for fraud, fine-tuned for deception, or simply general-purpose systems misused by scammers.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock, where Bullock supposedly became angry about questions regarding Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never actually occurred. This type of scam is becoming increasingly common, with artificial intelligence making it easier for fraudsters to create convincing fake content featuring well-known Australians.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports a significant rise in AI-generated investment scams using deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams, up 182 percent, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, financial presenter Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated figures. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that professional-looking content alone does not guarantee legitimacy.
